Learning Objectives
Assess the pathophysiology of cervical degeneration and axial neck pain.
Complete a thorough evaluation of patients with axial neck pain.
Determine appropriate diagnostic tests for patients with axial neck pain.
Develop a differential diagnosis for axial neck pain.
Formulate an appropriate treatment plan for the management of axial neck pain.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Mechanical neck pain in the absence of radiculopathy
Often, this type of mechanical pain is self-limiting and will resolve without major investigation


Overview
Axial neck pain is discomfort limited to the local myofascial or skeletal region of the neck
without radicular or myelopathic symptoms. Pain may occur in the occipital region, the
posterior cervical spine, or the periscapular region. Often, this type of mechanical pain is
self-limiting and will resolve without major investigation or management.
Epidemiology
The prevalence of axial neck pain in adults in North America is 66%.
Women are more commonly affected than men

Epidemiology
Degenerative cervical conditions are only slightly less common than low back pain.
Population studies have shown that the prevalence of axial neck pain in adults in North
America is 66%. Most of the symptoms of axial neck pain are mild and will resolve with
nonsurgical management. However, as much as 5% of the population will experience
debilitating symptoms, resulting in an increased likelihood of progression to chronic,
persistent axial pain1 (Resource 1). Women tend to experience axial neck pain more
frequently than men.
Etiology and Pathogenesis
Pathogenesis of cervical disk degeneration
With aging, the ratio of keratan sulfate to chondroitin sulfate increases and water content
decreases, leading to a cascade of secondary degenerative events (spondylosis).
These changes may result in increased segmental motion, compensatory osteophytes,
buckling of the ligamentum flavum, and facet arthrosis, all of which may cause axial neck
pain and/or neural impingement2 (Resource 2).


Etiology and Pathogenesis
Several pain generators are present in the neck, which often makes the diagnosis of neck
pain elusive. Axial pain may result from disk disease; facet degeneration, including
atlantoaxial arthrosis; neurologic compression, or muscular or ligamentous factors. A
myofascial etiology for neck pain may be the result of injury or poor
posture/ergonomics, stress, and fatigue.3
One of the most common causes of axial neck pain is cervical strain or injury to the soft
tissues (muscle, tendon, and ligaments) of the neck. Such an injury that occurs after
rapid acceleration-deceleration trauma is referred to as whiplash. The associated
pathogenesis is postulated to consist of small tears with resultant hematoma and
fibrosis in the muscles, anulus, facet capsules, etc.
Persistent neck pain, in the absence of trauma or other identifiable disease process,
often is attributed to cervical disk degeneration. The anulus contains nerve fibers, and
the disk pulp is innervated by the sinuvertebral nerve. Both have been implicated as pain
generators resulting in axial neck symptoms.4 Facet joint stress and inflammation also
are well-known causes that tend to result in mechanical neck pain.5 Most axial neck pain
is ascribed to subaxial degenerative pathology; however, in older patients, atlantoaxial
joint arthrosis may be a very specific cause of axial neck pain.
Natural History
Chronic neck pain affects 10% to 34% of the general population.
Most patients will improve with nonsurgical treatment.

Natural History
Chronic neck pain affects 10% to 34% of the general population. Approximately 50% of
these individuals will experience headaches in the occipital region.6 Most patients will

improve with nonsurgical treatment. After 3 months of nonsurgical treatment,
approximately 70% of patients will have experienced improvement, and as many as 22%
of patients will have no relief.7
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
Neck pain is a common presenting symptom.
Axial neck pain is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Critical to eliminate red-flag symptoms and any neurologic findings
A musculoskeletal examination of the neck and shoulders must be performed.

Evaluation and Diagnosis
Myofascial and axial neck pain is a common problem. Axial neck pain is a diagnosis of
exclusion because no validated or reliable tools and tests exist to pinpoint the exact
etiology in most patients. A detailed patient history is essential to rule out a more
ominous diagnosis. Attention should be paid to red-flag symptoms, such as night pain,
unremitting pain even at rest, fevers, weight loss, or antecedent infection or trauma.
Neurologic symptoms or deficits are not uncommon in patients with neck pain.
Therefore, a complete patient history and physical examination are essential. Symptoms
typically are episodic, with acute pain generally improving over days to weeks.
Symptoms may be exacerbated with range of motion and activity. A complete physical
examination of the cervical spine and shoulders should be performed. The
musculoskeletal examination should assess active and passive range of motion in flexion
and extension, lateral tilting, and rotation of the neck. Palpation may reproduce
symptoms and localize pain generators, including occipital structures, spinous
processes, facet joints, and myofascial triggers. A thorough neurologic examination also
should be performed to rule out radiculopathy, myelopathy, and concomitant peripheral
nerve compression (Figure 1).

Diagnostic Studies
Initial imaging studies, if indicated, should consist of plain radiographs.
Radiographic evidence of cervical spondylosis is very common in asymptomatic adults,
especially those older than 40 years.
Advanced imaging studies
CT
Used for assessment of fractures; stenosis as a result of bony impingement or calcified
processes, such as ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament; and asymmetric
spondylosis, which results from skeletal hyperostosis
MRI
Preferred imaging modality for evaluating disks, ligaments, muscles, marrow, and neural
elements in the cervical spine

Diagnostic Studies
Often, imaging and diagnostic studies are not required in patients with acute complaints
of axial neck pain; however, plain radiographs can be ordered for better evaluation of
patients with extended pain. Spondylotic changes are very common in adults.
Approximately 25% of individuals younger than 40 years, 50% of individuals older than
40 years, and 85% of individuals older than 60 years have some degree of disk
degeneration.
Other indications for plain radiography include a history of trauma, autoimmune disease
(ie, rheumatoid arthritis), or concern for infection. Radiographs should be obtained in
patients who delineate a history of or report constitutional symptoms or a systemic
disorder, such as cancer or inflammatory spondyloarthropathy. In addition, plain
radiographs should be obtained in patients with neurologic deficits or a history of
myelopathy and/or radiculopathy. AP radiographs may reveal degenerative changes in
the uncovertebral joints or coronal or rotatory deformity. AP radiographs also may
reveal osseous lesions. Lateral radiographs aid in assessing overall alignment (lordosis,
kyphosis), disk space narrowing, vertebral body osteophytes, and listhesis. Surgeons

must evaluate the soft-tissue shadows, particularly if concern for trauma or infection
exists. Oblique radiographs may aid in evaluating neuroforaminal stenosis or facet
arthrosis. Flexion-extension radiographs should be obtained to evaluate instability or to
investigate postoperative pseudarthrosis. Open-mouth odontoid radiographs may aid in
evaluating the upper cervical spine, specifically C1-C2 alignment and facet articulations.
Advanced imaging studies of the spine are considered in patients with persistent
symptoms of axial neck pain and patients in whom concern for neurologic impingement
or spinal instability exists. CT scans with appropriate sagittal, coronal, and oblique
reconstructions aid in delineating bony anatomy and alignment. CT is the best imaging
modality for assessing fractures and stenosis as a result of bony impingement or
calcified processes, such as ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament. In certain
patients, CT myelography is ordered. CT myelography can be performed to rule out
neural compression in patients who cannot undergo MRI and patients in whom MRI
artifact results from existing spinal instrumentation or extensive dental implants. MRI is
the best imaging modality for evaluating disks, ligaments, muscles, marrow, and neural
elements in the cervical spine. MRI with and without contrast is commonly performed to
evaluate and diagnose infections and neoplasms of the spine.
Radionuclide imaging, such as bone scanning or single photon emission computed
tomography, can be performed on the rare occasion that a patient requires treatment
for the management of axial neck pain. Bone scintigraphy is a very sensitive yet
nonspecific imaging modality that assesses change in blood flow or bone metabolism.
Bone scintigraphy is best utilized in patients undergoing work up for neoplastic or
infectious/metabolic pathology about the spine.
Differential Diagnosis

Differential Diagnosis
The various causes of neck pain should be ruled out before proceeding with
management for cervical spondylosis.1 The differential diagnosis for mechanical neck
pain includes musculoskeletal and nonorthopaedic conditions (Table 1).

Nondegenerative conditions that may result in axial neck pain include fractures,
dislocations, inflammatory arthritides (rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis),
infections (discitis, osteomyelitis, epidural abscess), and tumors (intradural, extradural).

Management
Most patients with axial neck pain respond favorably to nonsurgical treatment. Activity
modifications in combination with a brief period of rest or soft-collar immobilization may be
appropriate. If not contraindicated, NSAIDs, corticosteroids, and muscle relaxants may be
prescribed. Ice and heat also may be recommended to diminish medication intake. Physical
therapy focusing on isometric exercises, aerobic conditioning, and resistance training is helpful in
this patient population. The success rate for nonsurgical treatment in this patient population
ranges from 70% to 80%.7,8

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical treatment is preferred in patients with isolated axial neck pain resulting from
cervical spondylosis.
NSAIDs are commonly prescribed.
The routine use of opioid medications is not recommended.
Isometric cervical muscle strengthening, heat/ice/massage, and short-term immobilization in a
soft collar may be considered.
Injections may be considered as a second-line treatment option if nonsurgical treatment fails.

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical treatment is preferred in patients with axial neck pain. Initial nonsurgical
management may consist of NSAIDs and physical therapy, including isometric
strengthening, range of motion, and pain relief management. The routine use of opioid
medications is not recommended. If initial nonsurgical management fails, then cervical
injections may be used for diagnostic and potentially therapeutic purposes. These may
include medial branch blocks directed to the cervical facet joints or trigger point
injections aimed at myofascial triggers.
Surgical management is not considered a standard treatment option for conventional
axial neck pain and may only be considered on the rare occasion, such as in patients
with instability or a destructive process involving the disk space or the facet joints.
Posterior C1-C2 arthrodesis may be considered in patients diagnosed with C1-C2
instability or arthrosis with pain. Favorable posterior C1-C2 arthrodesis results have
been reported in highly selected patients with atlantoaxial osteoarthrosis in whom
nonsurgical treatment fails.
